claims.text: Temperature-dependent amplification of internal residual stresses causes the apparent discrepancies in the alloy's stress-strain and thermoelastic behavior.
The residual stresses are generated by differential thermal expansion at sub-grain interfaces formed during cold rolling and aging.
These internal stresses modulate the dislocation network and lattice distortion.
One residual-stress mechanism can unify changes in creep rate, hardness, and elastic moduli.
The as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase BCC solid solution.
Cold rolling introduces dislocation networks and nanoscale phase features into the alloy.
Heavy cold rolling produces a high dislocation density.
Heavy cold rolling causes a stress-induced phase transformation in HfNbTaTiZr.
Solution annealing minimizes processing-induced defects and internal residual stresses.
Aging produces precipitation that contributes to sub-grain boundary lattice distortion.
HfNbTaTiZr has an inherently high thermal expansion coefficient.
Increasing temperature increases differential strain between sub-grains and interfaces.
Thermal-expansion mismatch intensifies internal residual stresses in cold-rolled or aged samples with high dislocation densities.
The intensified residual stresses enhance dislocation pinning.
The intensified residual stresses alter lattice stiffness and elastic moduli.
The alloy exhibits high room-temperature yield strength and resistance to elevated-temperature softening.
Cold-rolled and aged samples will have greater room-temperature hardness and yield strength than solution-annealed samples.
Cold-rolled and aged samples will resist thermal softening more strongly than solution-annealed samples because residual stresses persist.
Cold-worked samples will exhibit greater effective thermal expansion than solution-annealed samples, and this expansion will correlate with elastic-modulus and creep changes.
The proposed residual-stress effect operates from 293 K to approximately 1250 °C and is strongest in high-dislocation-density microstructures.
